title: Wind sails, e-methanol and a stalled global deal: Can hard-to-decarbonise shipping go green?
summary: The IMO is again attempting a "Net-Zero Framework" for shipping, years after political interference stalled a global deal, ensuring prolonged reliance on high-carbon fuels. While discussing wind sails and e-methanol, the continued industry embrace of LNG—a fossil fuel—exposes a lack of commitment to genuine decarbonisation. This delayed action guarantees continued excessive HFO usage, escalating carbon intensity, and ensures ships will continue to exceed CII ratings, incurring significant FuelEU Maritime fines.
content:
A year after Trump stalled a global net-zero shipping deal, the IMO is trying again – with wind power, batteries, e-fuels and LNG in the mix.

Last year, the Trump administration derailed a global breakthrough aimed at cleaning up shipping, one of the world’s most difficult-to-decarbonise sectors. Now the International Maritime Organization (IMO) is trying again.

Between 23 November and 4 December, the UN agency will meet to discuss the sector’s future Net-Zero Framework. The decisions made will lock in the emissions profile of ships for the next 20+ years.

A framework including a global fuel standard and a pricing mechanism on greenhouse gas emissions from ships was already approved by IMO’s Marine Environment Protection Committee in spring 2025. It was scheduled for formal adoption in October 2025 – until the POTUS threatened to impose tariffs on all countries that supported it, leading further talks and decision-making to be postponed by a year.

Is there a fresh chance to get a global deal on shipping by the end of 2026? Could the Democrats’ recent victory in the midterm elections offer new momentum? Or will the Net-Zero Framework run aground once and for all?

Shipping is one of the hardest to abate sectors’

Euronews Earth spoke to stakeholders working towards deep decarbonisation of the sector. While they anticipate stormy weather along the course, there are also a few glimmers of hope on the more distant horizon.

Shipping moves more than 80 per cent of global trade by volume and is responsible for 2.3 per cent of global CO2 emissions, roughly the same as the entire annual emissions of Japan. Promising solutions already exist, but scaling them depends on infrastructure, investment and policy frameworks.

Shipping is one of the hardest to abate sectors”, says Dr Peter Schniering, CEO and co-founder of Future Cleantech Architects (FCA), a science-based non-profit organisation and innovation think tank headquartered in Germany. His colleague, FCA Cleantech Analyst Pauline Leroi, provided much of the data and analysis below.

About 90 per cent of the global shipping fleet runs on oil-based fuels. Tankers, container ships and bulk carriers are “the biggest polluters”, says Leroi, followed by cruise ships and general cargo ships. Together, those five vessel types are responsible for 664 million tonnes of CO2 emissions per year. Europe is responsible for 14 per cent of those shipping emissions (China 17 per cent, USA 9 per cent).

The majority of emissions come from large deep-sea shipping vessels. There are currently around 6,000 container ships sailing the world’s oceans and rivers, 8,200 oil tankers, some 13,000 bulk carriers and 960 ships used for tourism.

Wind assisted propulsion and onboard carbon capture: Tools for net-zero shipping

Leroi unpacks the different pathways to net-zero shipping, from alternative fuels to electrification and efficiency solutions, and explains the trade-offs behind them. Slow steaming would be an efficient first step, in her opinion, especially for container ships: “Steaming 10 per cent slower results in up to 20 per cent less fuel burnt.”

There is no magic nautical treasure map – it looks more like a jigsaw puzzle, combining several solutions that fit well together. “Efficiency improvements – such as better hydrodynamics, smarter logistics, upgraded machinery, digitalisation – can save five to 20 per cent of greenhouse gas emissions,” says Leroi. “Wind assisted propulsion systems and on-board carbon capture could save up to a further 25 per cent of GHG emissions.”

Wind-power assisted propulsion systems, such as rotor sails, suction sails or wing sails, could bring down GHG emissions by up to 30 per cent per nautical mile – if weather and wind conditions are favourable. That is mostly the case on busy transatlantic or transpacific routes: “There’s lots of wind around there, usually,” Leroi says.

However, “that’s not the best solution for container ships”, which already have containers piled up, leaving little room for high-towering systems. “But it would be good for tankers and bulk carriers.”

Some 150 ships already have wind assistance today. For tankers, combining wind assistance with shore power, plugging into the port’s electricity supply instead of running onboard generators while docked, could save up to 70 million tonnes of CO2 per year, Leroi says.

“The biggest GHG reduction, however, could come from changing marine fuels – up to 90 per cent reduction, as well as from new propulsion technologies, up to 100 per cent (battery-electric, battery hybridisation, nuclear)”, Leroi says.

Redesigning shipping ports for an electric future

Regarding electric battery solutions, Leroi is in favour and mentions China, which is already operating a 120-metre-long all-electric container vessel on the Yangtze, the world’s third-longest river. “Specifically smaller cargo vessels should all go electric,” she recommends. In a second wave, shorter and medium distance cargo shipping routes could opt for electric battery systems as well.

Smaller cargo vessels should all go electric. ‘’

Pauline Leroi, Cleantech Analyst, FCA

This needs a container battery swapping system at ports along the ship’s route: instead of bunkering oil or gas, cargo ships take onboard a container packed with batteries. Medium distances could get split, with stopovers enabling vessels to change empty container batteries for fully charged ones.

China leads on swappable container battery systems, but there are start-ups in Europe too. Battery swapping for container ships could save another 35 million tonnes of CO2 per year.

Dual fuel ships could switch from LNG to green alternatives in future

Even without a global IMO deal, a transition will go ahead in the shipping sector anyway, experts agree, albeit at a slower pace. That’s where the European Union steps in. “Let’s take ships running on heavy fuel oil,” Leroi explains: “Under FuelEU Maritime Regulation they will not be compliant by 2030 and European vessels will have to transition to lower carbon emitting fuels.”

“Until green fuels are available at scale, transitional fuels could offer only a limited bridging solution,” Leroi emphasises. “Today, liquefied Natural gas (LNG) is the most mature option” – but still far from perfect. While heavy fuel oil has lifecycle emissions of 92 grams of CO2-equivalent per megajoule, LNG still stands at 76g CO2e/MJ, a 25 per cent reduction. Many EU shipowners have opted for it, as it is compliant under the FuelEU Maritime Regulation and other regulations.

The EU’s FuelEU Maritime Regulation is currently the only fully working regulatory framework designed specifically to cut shipping emissions. Patrick Cummins-Tripodi, FCA’s Brussels-based Cleantech Policy Officer, calls the EU’s approach “a strong basis for greening the sector”, but points to the “fact that LNG-powered ships comply with the FuelEU Maritime Regulation”: as a result, “LNG continues to dominate the ship orderbook”.

Why is this an issue? “There is significant methane slip during onboard combustion as well as methane leakage during upstream fuel production and transition, which is not always accounted for,” Leroi warns.

EU shipping methane emissions rose by 30 per cent in 2025. That’s alarming considering that methane is around 80 times more potent at trapping heat than CO2 over a 20-year timeframe. Cummins-Tripodi adds that “methane emission values at the EU and IMO level do not account for the full impact of methane slip, which if updated could penalise the choice of LNG”.

Ships ordered today will operate well beyond 2050, so the order books show what shipowners are betting on. 78 per cent of vessel orders are still for conventional oil propulsion systems – almost 2,200 ships designed to run on fossil fuels. If shipowners move away from oil, they mostly opt for LNG (407 vessels ordered), then methanol (134), according to the 2025 order book.

“It is important to add that many of those ordered ships have a dual fuel design,” Leroi flags. Dual fuel ships designed for running on LNG, ‘grey methanol’ or on ‘grey ammonia’ – produced using fossil fuels – can later switch to ‘green methanol’ or ‘green ammonia’, produced using renewable energy sources.

“Being able to burn those alternative fuels does not mean that they necessarily will – some of those vessel types will continue to burn heavy fuel oil.”

Why can’t shipping rely on biofuels or e-fuels?

Why not just switch to biofuels, with lifecycle emissions of just 21g CO2eq/MJ?

“The main issue with biofuels when decarbonising the shipping sector is that the biofuels feedstock availability simply cannot meet the scale of shipping’s fuel demand. And they are three to four times more expensive,” explains Leroi.

And what about e-fuels, such as e-methanol, e-ammonia or liquid green hydrogen? “They can offer very significant reductions (in terms of GHG emissions) – but e-fuels are even six to seven times more expensive than heavy fuel oil, for instance.”

Leroi is sceptical about e-ammonia: “It is highly toxic to fish and the maritime environment in general.” Even so, she says low-carbon ammonia “could really cut a lot of emissions” on the largest bulk carriers and container ships, if toxicity and handling are addressed. On liquid green hydrogen, she points to “the very low energy density”, meaning more tanks would be required for the same energy output.

E-methanol, on the other hand, has the advantage that the propulsion technology works well and the technology readiness level is high. Its lifecycle emissions are low, just 28g CO2eq/MJ. But it still is prohibitively expensive, for the moment, because production is lagging behind.

Using it on cargo ships could cut up to an estimated 320 million tonnes of CO2 per year. Cruise ships could also be hybridised with low-carbon methanol, biomethanol or e-methanol, for a further 40 million tonnes, and Europe has “real leverage”, as 97 per cent of cruise ships are built here.

Why don’t e-fuel suppliers ramp up production?

Addressing the issues with production isn’t so simple: “Fuel producers need to know that vessels will buy green fuels. Ship owners need to know these fuels to be available before they order new vessels. And ports need to build bunkering infrastructure that connects the two,” Leroi explains.

One of those first movers is Knud Erik Andersen, co-founder and CEO of European Energy, a company in sustainable energy generation. It has invested heavily in battery storage, solar and wind power, and in Power-to-X facilities – plants producing sustainable e-fuels using renewable energy sources.

With the recently inaugurated Kasso site in Denmark, European Energy made headlines. It is the world’s first large-scale commercial e-methanol facility, with an annual production capacity of 42,000 tonnes – and operating entirely on solar energy. The plant, next to Northern Europe’s largest solar park, produces e-methanol with up to a 97 per cent reduced carbon footprint compared to fossil-based products.

We need long-term regulatory certainty that Europe sticks to these commitments and ambitions,” says Lars Dyrholm, CEO of the Kasso plant. “We have plans for more plants [but] when you make an investment as large as this, you really need certainty for the future income… No one will make an investment like this unless they are sure that the product produced can compete in the market.”

Andersen has a proposal: “Why shouldn’t the public sector in Europe buy e-fuels for naval ships, for the defence industry? The public sector could not only give support by grants and subsidy schemes, it could also act as a customer.”

Measures such as the sustainable maritime fuel allowances under the EU’s Emissions Trading System (ETS) “may help with the final cost, but it may not solve the chicken-and-egg problem” with supply and demand, Cummins-Tripodi says. Incentives and/or tough legal obligations are needed to ensure that all stakeholders take the necessary steps.

An e-fuel market still needs to be created, production needs to be scaled up globally, and the world is still waiting for a reliable international legal framework from the IMO.

Saving 280 tonnes of CO2 each day per ship

One of the biggest buyers of green methanol produced at Kasso is the Danish logistics group Maersk, which is converting part of its global fleet to sustainable fuels.

The world’s first methanol-enabled cargo ship, the 172-metre Laura Maersk, started service in 2023. This was followed in 2024 by Ane Maersk, a 350-metre container vessel carrying up to 16,000 containers when fully loaded. Compared to a sister ship powered by heavy fuel oil, the Ane Maersk saves 280 tonnes of CO2 per day.

Ten more dual-fuel methanol vessels joined the Maersk fleet in 2025, bringing the company’s total to 19 (out of some 700 vessels). The target for 2030 is 94 dual fuel vessels.

Maersk stresses the importance of global regulation – and deeply regrets the delay of adopting the Net-Zero Framework: “Our climate transition plan is significantly dependent on the regulatory landscape, especially our ability to shift to lower greenhouse gas emission fuels,” the company states. “This signature regulatory framework would lay the foundation for closing the price gap between lower GHG emission fuels and fossil-based fuels.”

Port Esbjerg wants to become an international benchmark for sustainability

At Port Esbjerg, where Denmark borders the North Sea, COO Jesper Bank says: “It’s quite clear for us from a strategic perspective that we have to be able to serve a multi-fuel market. But it is also very clear that this path forward is not clear, because you have many [fuelling] alternatives today.”

“The effort from the political side should not be on the technical issues – we will solve that. But it should be on creating the framework, the conditions for the market to develop,” Bank says.

He also calls for European alignment on hydrogen: “We need coordination of national hydrogen strategies. These are very different today: Sweden has one strategy, Denmark doesn’t really have one and Germany has still another one.”

The regulatory gap extends to ports, says Cummins-Tripodi: “Apart from the EU’s Alternative Fuels Infrastructure Regulation’s loose target for LNG, there is no obligation on ports or fuel suppliers to ensure the supply of alternative fuels.”

Uncertainty is increasing pressure on shipowners

Shipowners are adrift in an ocean of regulatory uncertainty. Some in-depth studies, such as classification society DNV’s 10th Maritime Forecast to 2050, alert that “regulatory uncertainty is increasing pressure on shipowners”.

It stresses the urgent need for “stronger global regulatory signals” that “could accelerate the uptake of energy-efficient measures, enabling the global fleet to consume up to 25 per cent less energy by 2050 compared to a scenario where regulation is driven [only] by regions”.

The global Net-Zero Framework

Getting the global Net-Zero Framework adopted would create a pricing mechanism with set prices on the greenhouse gases ships emit, to encourage the industry to lower emissions to comply with a global fuel standard. It would apply to all oceangoing ships over 5,000 gross tonnage – the vessels responsible for over 85 per cent of global shipping emissions – and IMO’s Marine Environment Protection Committee would set up a Sustainable Fuel Certification Scheme to make sure fuel emissions and sustainability get independently verified.

If the greenhouse gas fuel intensity is too high, a price has to be paid. If a ship emits below a certain threshold or switches to zero or near-zero emission fuels, it will get financially rewarded. IMO could set up a Net Zero Fund, collecting revenue from non-compliant, heavily polluting ships to reward low-emission ships.

It should not really be called a global carbon tax, the IMO insists. It would be more of a performance-based GHG-intensity target system: vessels that exceed pollution limits must pay tiered compliance fees, while those that outperform can earn tradeable credits and be eligible for rewards.

Cummins-Tripodi isn’t optimistic about the talks. “Last year’s proposal will probably not survive,” he says. “It is highly unlikely.”

The IMO deal to some extent mirrors the EU’s approach, including a greenhouse gas intensity reduction target for shipping, but he warns of a shortcoming: “it could be cheaper for companies to pay penalties instead of complying”.
